\chapter*{Italian pronunciation --- a reference}
\addcontentsline{toc}{chapter}{Italian pronunciation (reference)}
\markboth{Pronunciation}{Pronunciation}

A \textbf{reference}, not a chapter — each lesson gives the sounds its word needs; this page gathers them. Italian is gloriously \textbf{phonetic}: learn these rules and you can read almost any word aloud correctly.

\section*{The traps for an English speaker}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
\setlength{\itemsep}{0.35em}
  \item \textbf{Every letter is sounded}, and vowels are pure: \emph{a} (ah), \emph{e} (eh), \emph{i} (ee), \emph{o} (oh), \emph{u} (oo) — never the English glide.
  \item \textbf{c} and \textbf{g} are soft (\emph{ch}, \emph{j}) before \emph{e/i} (\emph{ciao}, \emph{giorno}), hard (\emph{k}, \emph{g}) before \emph{a/o/u} (\emph{casa}, \emph{gatto}). \textbf{ch}/\textbf{gh} force the hard sound (\emph{chi} = \textquotedblleft{}kee\textquotedblright{}).
  \item \textbf{gli} = the \emph{lli} of \emph{million}; \textbf{gn} = the \emph{ny} of \emph{canyon}; \textbf{sc} before \emph{e/i} = \emph{sh} (\emph{sciare} = \textquotedblleft{}shee-AH-reh\textquotedblright{}).
  \item \textbf{z} = \emph{ts} or \emph{dz} (\emph{grazie} = \textquotedblleft{}GRAH-tsyeh\textquotedblright{}).
  \item \textbf{Double consonants are held longer} and change meaning: \emph{no\textbf{tt}e} (night) vs. \emph{note} (notes); \emph{no\textbf{nn}o} (grandfather) vs. \emph{nono} (ninth).
  \item \textbf{h} is always silent — it exists only to harden \emph{c}/\emph{g}.
\end{itemize}

\section*{Stress}

Most words stress the \textbf{second-to-last} syllable (\emph{giOR-no}). When the stress falls on the last syllable it carries a written accent (\emph{città}, \emph{così}, \emph{caffè}).

\section*{Italian in the Romance family}

Italian, Spanish, and French are all worn-down Latin. Italian stayed closest to the parent: Latin \emph{-ct-} became \emph{-tt-} (\emph{notte}) where Spanish went \emph{-ch-} (\emph{noche}) and French \emph{-it-} (\emph{nuit}); and Italian kept final vowels (\emph{giorno}, \emph{notte}) that French dropped. The lessons draw these contrasts as they arise.
